question: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project I noticed a teammate kept missing code review deadlines. I asked if we could chat after standup and said the delays were blocking my work. We agreed on a shared checklist and daily check-ins for two weeks.
What was their reaction and how did it end?
They were defensive at first but the checklist helped. Deliverables improved and my manager later said it showed good ownership.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: teammate missing code review deadlines on first project
Action: asked for chat, shared impact, created shared checklist + daily check-ins
Outcome: defensiveness faded, deliverables improved, manager noted ownership
Quote: "the checklist helped"
Follow-up: What was their reaction and how did it end? -> described improvement and manager feedback
junior.raiseFeedback: The candidate described holding a peer accountable on an individual task by sharing impact and creating a simple process. They owned the follow-through and tied it to manager feedback. This meets junior expectations for coachability and local ownership. The story stayed within their own work rather than escalating. Biggest strength is the willingness to have the direct conversation instead of avoiding it.

lowerTranscript.text: I once saw someone on my team submitting late work but I didn't want to cause drama so I just picked up the slack myself.
Did you ever speak with them?
No, I figured it wasn't my place and the project still shipped.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: teammate submitting late work
Action: picked up slack without speaking to them
Outcome: project shipped but no conversation occurred
Quote: "I figured it wasn't my place"
Follow-up: Did you ever speak with them? -> avoided entirely
junior.lowerFeedback: The candidate avoided any direct conversation and absorbed the impact themselves. No evidence of attempting accountability or seeking guidance on how to handle it. This lowers the bar for junior because it shows lack of ownership even at the individual-contributor level. The core gap is unwillingness to address performance issues directly.

raiseTranscript.text: A partner team was consistently late delivering API changes that blocked our launch. I scheduled a 1:1 with their tech lead, shared the timeline impact with data, and we aligned on a joint milestone tracker.
How did you influence without authority?
I focused on shared launch risk and offered to help prioritize their work in our planning. The tracker made misses visible to both leads and we hit the date.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: partner team late on API changes blocking launch
Action: 1:1 with tech lead, shared data, created joint milestone tracker
Outcome: tracker made misses visible, launch date hit
Quote: "focused on shared launch risk"
Follow-up: How did you influence without authority? -> used shared risk and offered help
senior.raiseFeedback: Candidate handled cross-team underperformance by using data and shared goals rather than escalation. They created a lightweight mechanism that made accountability visible without authority. Story shows influence at the senior scope. Biggest strength is turning a blocking issue into a joint process that both sides adopted.

lowerTranscript.text: I escalated to my manager when another team missed their commitments and let leadership sort it out.
Did you have any direct conversation first?
I sent a couple of emails but didn't want to step on toes so I went through the chain.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: another team missed commitments
Action: sent emails then escalated to manager
Outcome: handed off to leadership
Quote: "didn't want to step on toes"
Follow-up: Did you have any direct conversation first? -> minimal direct effort
senior.lowerFeedback: Candidate defaulted to escalation and avoided direct accountability conversation. No attempt to use influence or create joint visibility. This lowers the bar at senior level where cross-team impact is expected. The gap is reliance on hierarchy instead of building alignment.

raiseTranscript.text: One of my engineers was missing sprint commitments repeatedly. I had a direct conversation with specific examples, asked for their view, and we set a 30-day improvement plan with weekly check-ins and clear deliverables.
They improved on two of three metrics. I documented everything and later used the record when giving a lower rating. The team saw that expectations were enforced.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: direct report missing sprint commitments
Action: direct conversation with examples, co-created 30-day plan with weekly check-ins
Outcome: partial improvement, used record for lower rating, team saw expectations enforced
Quote: "the team saw that expectations were enforced"
Follow-up: What happened after the plan? -> documented outcome and rating impact
manager.raiseFeedback: Candidate owned the full accountability loop including documentation and rating consequences. They involved the person in the plan while keeping clear ownership of team standards. This meets manager expectations for handling underperformance directly. Biggest strength is linking the conversation to visible team-level signal that standards apply to everyone.

lowerTranscript.text: I gave the underperformer a lot of coaching but never put anything in writing or changed their scope.
Did performance improve or did you adjust their rating?
It stayed the same so I just worked around it with the rest of the team.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: direct report underperforming
Action: informal coaching without documentation or scope change
Outcome: performance unchanged, worked around it
Quote: "just worked around it"
Follow-up: Did performance improve or did you adjust their rating? -> no formal action
manager.lowerFeedback: Candidate relied on informal coaching without documentation or consequences. No evidence of protecting team standards or addressing the issue at the rating level. This lowers the bar for a manager because underperformance handling stayed private and ineffective. The gap is lack of leverage through formal mechanisms.

raiseTranscript.text: Our sales org was missing quarterly targets because engineering was deprioritizing requested features. I brought both VPs together, showed the revenue impact, and we agreed on a shared OKR with bi-weekly reviews that I owned.
How did you handle resistance from the engineering side?
I accepted their resource constraints and shifted two roadmap items to later quarters. The joint OKR made the trade-off visible at the exec level and revenue recovered the next quarter.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: sales missing targets due to engineering deprioritization
Action: joint VP meeting, showed revenue data, created shared OKR with bi-weekly reviews
Outcome: accepted trade-offs, revenue recovered next quarter
Quote: "made the trade-off visible at the exec level"
Follow-up: How did you handle resistance from the engineering side? -> made trade-offs explicit
exec.raiseFeedback: Candidate addressed org-level misalignment by creating a cross-functional mechanism and owning the reviews. They made strategic trade-offs visible rather than forcing compliance. This meets exec expectations for using influence at the business level. Biggest strength is turning a recurring conflict into a durable process with measurable revenue impact.

lowerTranscript.text: I told the other VP their team needed to do better and asked HR to get involved.
What structural change did you make?
None, I expected them to fix their own execution.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you had to hold someone accountable for underperformance. How did you handle the conversation?
Situation: another org missing commitments
Action: told VP to do better and involved HR
Outcome: no structural change
Quote: "expected them to fix their own execution"
Follow-up: What structural change did you make? -> none
exec.lowerFeedback: Candidate treated the issue as a one-off conversation and delegated to HR without creating any joint mechanism. No evidence of strategic trade-offs or org-level leverage. This lowers the bar at exec level where the expectation is durable cross-org alignment. The gap is absence of systemic ownership.

diagnostic.junior: Raises when candidate initiates simple peer conversation
diagnostic.senior: Raises when candidate uses data and joint process without authority
diagnostic.manager: Raises when candidate creates documented improvement plan with consequences
diagnostic.exec: Raises when candidate builds cross-org mechanism with trade-offs

diagnostic.manager: Keeps clear ownership while involving the person
